extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of philosophy, metaphysics, and comparative religion
extracted.subtask_description: Close argumentative exposition on metaphysics, ethics, mysticism, and asceticism comparing Christianity, Brahmanism, Buddhism, and Sufism; presents methodological claims about philosophy and criteria for evaluating mystical claims and religious practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Philosophy's methodological standard
rubrics_metrics.description: The value and worth of philosophy lies in the fact that it rejects all assumptions which cannot be established, and takes as its data only what can be certainly proved in the world given in external perception, in the forms of apprehension of this world, which are constitutive of our intellect, and in the consciousness of one’s own self which is common to all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophy must 'beware of falling into the way of the mystics' by asserting intellectual intuitions or pretended immediate apprehensions of the reason. It 'must remain cosmology, and cannot become theology.' Its theme must limit itself to the world and express what the world is in its inmost nature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criterion distinguishing mystic and philosopher
rubrics_metrics.description: The mystic begins from within (inner, positive, individual experience) and cannot convince others since his testimony is private; the philosopher begins from without (objective phenomenon common to all) and can convince by reflection and combination of data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because mystical claims are grounded in private experience, they can only be accepted 'upon his word' and thus are not convincing; philosophical claims must be communicable and testable by shared forms of consciousness and perception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of asserting inaccessible positive knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: The philosopher ought to avoid making assertions of intellectual intuitions or pretended immediate apprehensions of the reason to display positive knowledge of what is forever inaccessible to knowledge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such assertions are a fall into mysticism; philosophy should express limits via negation where knowledge ceases, rather than claim positive metaphysical knowledge beyond perception and conception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Moral virtues as means, not ultimate ends
rubrics_metrics.description: Moral virtues (justice, benevolence/caritas) are not the ultimate end but only a step toward the denial of the will to live; they signify disillusionment with individual willing and serve as means advancing self-renunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Justice is described as 'the hair shirt that constantly harasses its owner' because pure justice and charity lead to sacrifice, suffering, and hence resignation; benevolence often accelerates renunciation because the benefactor takes on others' suffering.

rubrics_metrics.name: Asceticism's proper role and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Ascetic practices (celibacy, voluntary poverty, humility, obedience, abstention from animal food) are ways of advancing denial of the will to live; excessive self-mortification is rejected by Buddhism and may be superfluous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While asceticism (in the narrow sense: self-mortification, scourge, hair shirt) is historically present, Buddhism favors moderation—celibacy, poverty, humility—over extreme mortification. The moral virtues themselves introduce privation and suffering and can lead into asceticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Original sin / guilt of existence
rubrics_metrics.description: There is an assumed guilt intrinsic to existence: 'the greatest guilt of man is that he was born'; salvation requires a complete transformation (new birth) because works do not justify.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This claim is used to explain why moral actions cannot by themselves render one 'happy' or save one from suffering; doctrines (Christianity, Brahmanism, Buddhism) treat human existence as tainted and needing radical change or emancipation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mysticism signals the limit of conceptual knowledge
rubrics_metrics.description: All religions at their highest point pass over into mysticism and mysteries—into darkness and veiled obscurity—which for knowledge signify an empty spot where knowledge necessarily ceases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mysticism is 'every guidance to the immediate consciousness of that to which neither perception nor conception, thus in general no knowledge extends.' Philosophy should indicate such limits by negation rather than posit positive metaphysical content.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authenticity criterion from cross-cultural agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: The striking agreement among mystics and ascetics of diverse ages, countries, and religions—despite independent origins—serves as evidence that they speak from real inward experience (the work of grace) rather than mere imposture or madness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Similar doctrines found in widely separated cultures (e.g., Vedas, Christian mystics, Sufis) are taken to corroborate the inward experiential reality of mysticism; readers are urged to read mystics themselves rather than rely on secondhand reports.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character of mysticism differs by tradition
rubrics_metrics.description: Different religious traditions yield different tones of mysticism: Mohammedan (Sufi) mysticism is serene, Christian mysticism is gloomy and melancholy, Hindu mysticism stands above both and holds the mean.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a descriptive-evaluative standard when comparing mystic traditions; it informs expectations about emphasis (e.g., surrender vs. revelling in unity) and appropriate practices (e.g., suspension of thought in Brahmanism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Genuine Christianity's ascetic criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: True, original Christianity is characterized by an ascetic fundamental character—renunciation, self-denial, perfect chastity, mortification of the will—and recommends celibacy and virginity as the higher consecration.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The historical Church Fathers (Athanasius, Tertullian, Augustine, etc.) viewed marriage as a concession to human weakness and celibacy as the ideal; 'genuine Christianity' is judged by its tendency toward renunciation and ascetic practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Endpoint of intelligence and philosophy: negation
rubrics_metrics.description: Even the most perfect intelligence, faced with the tautology of fully comprehended nature across endless time, would see the only meaningful end as the reaction upon and abolition of willing; thus philosophy at its highest point assumes a negative character and ends with a negation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Philosophical inquiry discovers its limit in a 'relative, not an absolute nothing'—what can be asserted about the ultimate is only negative; mysticism provides the positive supplement but cannot be philosophical proof.
